stem:
A breastfeeding woman, eight weeks after birth, has taken oral flucloxacillin for mastitis for three days. Her fever has settled, but a tender, firm 4 cm swelling persists in the upper outer quadrant of the breast with overlying redness. She is otherwise well and is still feeding from both breasts.

Which investigation should be arranged next?

options.label: A
options.text: Diagnostic mammography to exclude an underlying malignancy
options.explanation: Mammography is uncomfortable and hard to interpret in an inflamed lactating breast, and it does not answer whether there is a drainable collection.

options.label: B
options.text: Ultrasound of the affected breast to look for a collection
options.explanation: A persistent localised mass after antibiotics suggests a breast abscess. Ultrasound confirms a collection and guides needle aspiration or drainage.

options.label: C
options.text: Breast-milk culture alone, continuing antibiotics until it settles
options.explanation: Milk culture can guide antibiotic choice when mastitis fails to respond, but on its own it cannot show whether a collection needs drainage.

options.label: D
options.text: Full blood count, CRP and blood cultures to track the infection
options.explanation: Blood tests may reflect inflammation, but they cannot show a collection or guide drainage, and she is systemically well.

options.label: E
options.text: Contrast-enhanced breast MRI to map the extent of inflammation
options.explanation: MRI is not a first-line test for a suspected lactational abscess; ultrasound answers the question quickly and can guide treatment.

context: A persistent breast lump after antibiotics for lactational mastitis needs ultrasound to look for an abscess that can be aspirated or drained.
